title: Dietary Patterns Are Not Consistently Associated with Variability in Blood Lead Concentrations in Pregnant British Women.
ehr_evidence: The primary source of data collection was self-completed questionnaires sent to the mother. Blood samples were collected by midwives during pregnancy. (Data derived from the ALSPAC UK birth cohort.)
summary: A birth-cohort study of 2167 pregnant British women from ALSPAC examined associations between dietary patterns and food groups (from a food-frequency questionnaire) and blood lead concentration, finding limited and inconsistent associations.
key_findings: The 'confectionery' dietary pattern was negatively associated with the likelihood of B-Pb ≥5 µg/dL in the adjusted model 2 (OR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.41, 0.94).
No associations were found for the other dietary patterns (healthy, traditional, processed, vegetarian).
The food group 'all leafy green and green vegetables' was positively associated with the likelihood of B-Pb ≥5 µg/dL (OR 1.45; 95% CI: 1.04, 2.01).
The food group 'cakes and biscuits' was negatively associated with B-Pb ≥5 µg/dL (OR 0.63; 95% CI: 0.43, 0.93).
After multiple imputation, a positive association of the 'healthy' diet pattern with B-Pb ≥5 µg/dL was found (Q4 vs Q1; OR: 1.58; 95% CI: 1.27, 1.97).
With B-Pb as a continuous variable, there were no associations with any dietary patterns; negative associations remained for 'cakes and biscuits' and 'milk'.
captured_features: Dietary pattern scores (healthy, traditional, processed, confectionery, vegetarian) derived by principal components analysis
Food group consumption frequencies (meats, fish, pulses, nuts, soybean products, root vegetables, leafy greens, breads and cereals, cakes and biscuits, pastas and rice)
Blood lead concentration dichotomized (<5 and ≥5 µg/dL)
Maternal age, education, Townsend score, BMI, energy intake, alcohol consumption, smoking status, hemoglobin
study_design: Birth cohort (ALSPAC); cross-sectional analysis of diet and blood lead
population: Pregnant women from the ALSPAC birth cohort in Avon, UK; complete-case analysis n=2167; maternal age roughly 19–35+ years
exposure_domain: Dietary patterns and food groups (diet); outcome is heavy metal (lead) exposure
limitations: Urban UK population with limited generalizability and relatively low lead exposure.
Temporal mismatch: blood sampled in first trimester while dietary data collected in third trimester, limiting causal inference.
Selection bias: included subsample differed sociodemographically from excluded participants.
data_availability_statement: University of Bristol: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. [Internet]. Available from: http://www.bristol.ac.uk/alspac/researchers/access/
